classification.difficultyReason: Students must distinguish whether a given quantity represents the total, one person's share or the difference. The hardest cases translate 'more than' into the difference of ratio parts before finding Jack's share using the taught method.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Kate and Jack share 24 sweets in the ratio $1:3$.
How many sweets does Kate get?

answer.worked:
Total parts: $1+3=4$.
$$\begin{align*}4\text{ parts}&=24\text{ sweets}\\1\text{ part}&=(24\div4)\text{ sweets}\\1\text{ part}&=6\text{ sweets}\end{align*}$$
Kate gets 6 sweets.

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Kate and Jack share 24 sweets in the ratio $3:1$.
How many sweets does Kate get?

answer.worked:
Total parts: $3+1=4$.
$$\begin{align*}4\text{ parts}&=24\text{ sweets}\\1\text{ part}&=(24\div4)\text{ sweets}=6\text{ sweets}\\3\text{ parts}&=(3\times6)\text{ sweets}=18\text{ sweets}\end{align*}$$
Kate gets 18 sweets.

Kate gets 18 sweets.

children.label: g
children.prompt:
Kate and Jack share some sweets in the ratio $3:1$.
Kate gets 12 more than Jack. How many does Jack get?

answer.worked:
The difference represents $3-1=2$ parts.
$$\begin{align*}2\text{ parts}&=12\text{ sweets}\\1\text{ part}&=(12\div2)\text{ sweets}=6\text{ sweets}\end{align*}$$
Jack gets 1 part, so he gets 6 sweets.

answer.worked:

They have 75 sweets altogether.

children.label: k
children.prompt:
Kate and Jack share some sweets in the ratio $4:1$.
What fraction of the sweets does Jack have?

answer.worked:

Jack has 1 of the 5 parts, so his fraction is $\frac{1}{5}$.
